statement: Chirikure, Pollard, Manyanga, and Bandama, "A Bayesian Chronology for Great Zimbabwe: Re-threading the Sequence of a Vandalised Monument," Antiquity 87 (2013): 1-19, re-analyzes radiocarbon dates against limited surviving stratigraphy (much of the original stratigraphy was destroyed by Richard Nicklin Hall's 1902-4 excavation) plus datable imports, using Bayesian statistical modeling. Dry-stone-wall construction begins c. 1200 CE (later than the older, still-popular "11th century" framing, which better fits early settlement rather than stone building specifically), reaching architectural peak in the 14th-15th centuries, with occupation continuing into the 16th and possibly 17th century. Cross-dating evidence: imported Chinese porcelain/celadon, Persian faience, Arabian glass, and Indian glass beads, corroborating the medieval date range via the Sofala/Kilwa Indian Ocean gold-trade network — though a dedicated porcelain-typology publication was not independently verified in this research pass.

sources.citation: Chirikure, S., M. Pollard, M. Manyanga, and F. Bandama. "A Bayesian Chronology for Great Zimbabwe: Re-threading the Sequence of a Vandalised Monument." Antiquity 87, 2013: 1-19.
